## 2

I understand why some images might seem suspicious—photos can be edited, and space agencies do release composite images. But the evidence for a spherical Earth doesn’t depend on trusting any one agency. We can observe ships disappearing hull-first over the horizon, different stars visible from different latitudes, Earth’s curved shadow during lunar eclipses, time zones, and satellite communication. These observations all fit a roughly spherical Earth and are difficult to explain consistently with a flat one.

## 3

Sunlight looks white, but it is actually made of many colors. When sunlight enters Earth’s atmosphere, it bumps into tiny air molecules. Blue light gets scattered in all directions more strongly than red, orange, or yellow light, so blue light reaches our eyes from across the sky.

At sunset, sunlight travels through much more atmosphere. Along the longer path, much of the blue light gets scattered away before it reaches us, leaving more reds and oranges. That is why the sky often turns warm-colored in the evening.
